title.text: AI that sees and reads: images, documents and speech

objects.text: What can AI see or read for us, and when should we not trust what it sees?

Leading with AI  |  Session 1 of the 15 (Sessions 0 to 14)
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. In Session 0 we drew the map: AI as a family, a model that learns from examples the way a new employee learns from past files, and the four jobs AI does. Today takes the first job, seeing and reading. Our question: what can AI see or read for us, and when should we not trust what it sees?

We start with a phone app built at Makerere, build the idea one picture at a time with no maths, tour six industries, and watch a small network learn to read handwriting. Then you add a use of your own to your AI Opportunity Portfolio.

title.text: What you will leave with today

objects.text: By the end of today you will have

objects.alt: plant

objects.text: Explain how a model learns to see from labelled photos, and why reading documents and turning speech into text are the same idea

objects.alt: question

objects.text: Spot when a seeing or reading system will struggle: a new picture unlike its examples, poor images, something it never saw

objects.alt: folder

objects.text: Add one place where AI could see or read for you to your AI Opportunity Portfolio

slides.notes:
That question breaks into three things you will be able to do by the end. You will be able to explain how a model learns to see from labelled photos, and why reading a document and turning speech into text are the same idea. You will spot when such a system will struggle, before a vendor tells you.

And your portfolio will hold one place in your organisation where AI could see or read for you.

title.text:
Your two hours: the idea, the industries,
a demonstration, then your own portfolio

objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: I run a recorded demonstration and one live one. You add a use to your own portfolio.

slides.notes:
Ten minutes to connect with Session 0 and meet today’s question. Forty minutes on the idea, one picture at a time, then the tour of six industries and three real cases. Fifteen minutes of demonstration: a recorded network that learned to read handwriting, and a live try with a receipt.

A five-minute break. Ten minutes on your people and the questions to ask. Then twenty-five minutes on your own portfolio, five on your decision, and ten to close.

title.text: Two questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  In Session 0, how does a model learn?
2.  What are the four jobs AI does?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Two quick questions from Session 0. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. 

Question one. In Session 0, how does a model learn? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. From past examples whose outcome is known, the way a new employee learns from past files.

Question two. What are the four jobs AI does? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. See and read, predict, understand and write language, and act.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet has it.

title.text: What today builds on, and where it leads

objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14; the gold one is today.

Today uses a model learns from examples from Session 0 and your chosen industry from Session 0.

It adds aI that sees images, reads documents, hears speech.

Session 2: the same learning, on your records.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Word
What it means
Pixel
One dot of a picture. The computer reads each dot as a number.
Training data
The labelled examples a model learns from, such as photos marked healthy or diseased.
Neural network
A model built in layers that finds small details, then shapes, then the answer.
OCR
Optical character recognition: software that reads printed or handwritten letters from a scan or photo.
Speech recognition
Software that turns recorded speech into written text, also called speech-to-text.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. We use every one of them before the end of the session.

Pixel. One dot of a picture. The computer reads each dot as a number.

Training data. The labelled examples a model learns from, such as photos marked healthy or diseased.

Neural network. A model built in layers that finds small details, then shapes, then the answer.

OCR. Optical character recognition: software that reads printed or handwritten letters from a scan or photo.

Speech recognition. Software that turns recorded speech into written text, also called speech-to-text.

title.text:
The model that learned from past files in Session
0 can learn from photos, pages and recordings

objects.alt: The model that learned from past files in Session 0 can learn from photos, pages and recordings

objects.text: Swap the files for photos and the outcome for what an expert says each one shows.

runs.text: Seeing and reading is the first of Session 0’s four jobs.

slides.notes:
Those five words rest on one idea you already hold. In Session 0 a model learned the way a new employee learns from past files: each file carried its outcome, repaid or not, and the model found the pattern. That is the left half of the slide. The right half is today.

Swap the files for photos of leaves, scanned forms or recorded speech, and swap the outcome for what an expert says the photo shows, or what the page or the voice says. Nothing else changes. Seeing and reading is the first of the four jobs, and a team in Kampala has already built one.

title.text:
A Makerere phone app names cassava
disease from a photo of the plant

objects.alt: A Makerere phone app names cassava disease from a photo of the plant

objects.text: Built in Kampala with the national crops research institute, for farmers and extension workers.

runs.text: Our question today: what can AI see or read for us, and when should we not trust it?

slides.notes:
The Makerere University AI lab built the app with the national crops research institute. A farmer or extension worker photographs the plant, and the app says healthy, or names one of the main cassava diseases, with an estimate of how severe. Farmers’ photos also carried their location, so researchers could map where disease spread.

The lead researcher reports about 400 downloads of the published model, and that light readings from the leaf spotted disease about six weeks before photos could. It was a research project, and no farm-level result was published. So how can a phone tell a sick leaf from a healthy one?

title.text:
To a computer, a photo is a grid
of dots, and every dot is a number

objects.alt: To a computer, a photo is a grid of dots, and every dot is a number

objects.text: The machine never sees a leaf or a letter, only numbers.

runs.text: A colour phone photo is millions of numbers, three for every dot.

slides.notes:
Start with what the phone receives. It never sees a leaf the way you do. It gets a grid of dots, which the industry calls pixels, and each dot is a number. On the left is a handwritten 3 from today’s demonstration, as you see it. On the right is what the computer gets: 64 numbers, 0 for blank paper and 16 for full ink.

A colour photo works the same way, with three numbers per dot for red, green and blue, so a photo a thousand dots wide and a thousand high is three million numbers. For a machine, seeing means finding patterns in those numbers, and it learns which patterns matter from examples.

title.text:
It learns from thousands of photos
that experts have already labelled

objects.alt: It learns from thousands of photos that experts have already labelled

objects.text: If the experts labelled wrongly, the model learns their mistakes.

runs.text: The labelled photos are called the training data.
The 9 in 10 on the slide is illustrative.

slides.notes:
The learning works as in Session 0. An apprentice agronomist learns by sitting with a senior expert who shows thousands of leaves and says each time: healthy, diseased, diseased, healthy. After enough of them, the apprentice can judge a new leaf alone. A model learns the same way.

Experts label thousands of photos, and the industry calls that labelled set the training data. The model looks for the signs that go with each label, brown spots, yellow edges, and then judges a photo it has never seen, giving a likelihood such as 9 in 10 diseased. That figure is illustrative. Everything rests on the labels.

title.text:
It looks in layers, and each layer builds
larger shapes from the one before

objects.alt: It looks in layers, and each layer builds larger shapes from the one before

objects.text: The industry calls this a neural network; many layers make it deep learning.

runs.text: Nobody writes these steps. The network adjusts itself, photo after photo, until its answers match the labels.

slides.notes:
How does it find those signs?

In layers, a little like your own eye and brain. The first layer looks at small groups of dots and picks out edges and specks. The next combines those into larger things: a spot, a patch, the edge of a leaf. The last layer weighs what it found and gives the answer, diseased.

A model built like this is called a neural network, and one with many layers is what people mean by deep learning. Nobody writes these steps. The network adjusts itself, photo after photo, until its answers match the labels, and in today’s demonstration you will watch one do it.

title.text:
Reading a document works the same
way, because every letter is a small image

objects.alt: Reading a document works the same way, because every letter is a small image

objects.text: The industry calls it OCR, optical character recognition.

runs.text: It learned from pages whose words were already typed out.
Handwriting, stamps and creases make it harder.

slides.notes:
Pages belong in today’s session for the same reason. A scanned form or a phone photo of a receipt is also a grid of dots. Each letter or figure is a small image, and a model that learned from thousands of pages whose words were already typed out can say: that shape is a 2.

The industry calls this OCR, optical character recognition. Modern tools go one step further and put each value in its place: farmer, bags, date. The good ones also mark the fields they are unsure of, in gold here, so a person checks them. Handwriting, stamps and creases make the work harder.

title.text:
Speech-to-text first draws the sound as
an image, then reads it the same way

objects.alt: Speech-to-text first draws the sound as an image, then reads it the same way

objects.text: The industry calls it speech recognition, or speech-to-text.

runs.text: It learned from hours of speech with typed transcripts.
Luganda, Runyankole and Swahili have far fewer recordings than English.

slides.notes:
The third input is the human voice. A recording is a wave of sound, and the system first turns it into an image of the sound, light and dark bands showing which tones were loud at each moment. Then, as with leaves and letters, a model that learned from many hours of recordings with typed transcripts says which words that image holds.

The industry calls this speech recognition, or speech-to-text. The words in the gold box are an illustration. One warning for East Africa: there are far fewer recordings in Luganda, Runyankole or Swahili than in English, so quality varies. Session 4 returns to local languages.

title.text:
Photos, pages and recordings differ only
in what goes in; the learning is the same

objects.alt: Photos, pages and recordings differ only in what goes in; the learning is the same

objects.text: Each model on the slide learned from examples that people had labelled by hand.

slides.notes:
Set side by side, the three differ only in what goes in. Given a photo of a leaf, a model that learned from thousands of photos labelled healthy or diseased gives back a label. Given a scanned page, a model that learned from pages with their words typed out gives back the words, ready for a table.

Given a recording, a model that learned from hours of speech with transcripts gives back a transcript. Reading documents and turning speech into text are therefore no new ideas. They are one idea, learning from labelled examples, applied to a different input. And because they share the idea, they share the same strengths and the same weak spots.

title.text:
It is good at volume and consistency, and struggles
when a new photo differs from its examples

objects.alt: It is good at volume and consistency, and struggles when a new photo differs from its examples

objects.text: It knows only the kind of images it learned from.

runs.text: The right-hand list is the one to keep.

slides.notes:
They are good at volume: thousands of images or pages a day, each read with the same care at five in the evening as at nine in the morning. They turn paper and speech into data a system can use, they run on a phone where experts are few, and they sort the clear cases from the doubtful.

They struggle when the new image differs from the examples: another camera, poor light, a different angle, a blurred or smudged image, an accent they rarely heard, or something they never saw at all. Keep that second list. A field study in Thai clinics shows it at work.

title.text:
Google’s eye screening scored 90% in its own tests;
in clinics, dark and blurred photos were turned away

objects.alt: Google’s eye screening scored 90% in its own tests; in clinics, dark and blurred photos were turned away

objects.text: The tests and the clinic were different worlds.

runs.text: An early field study, published by Google itself.
It does not mean the product later failed.

slides.notes:
Google Health worked with Thailand’s Ministry of Public Health on screening diabetic patients for eye disease. A nurse photographs the back of the eye, and the system grades it in about a minute. In Google’s internal tests it showed 90 per cent accuracy. Then, in eleven real clinics, it rejected photos that were blurred or dark, and only some clinics had a room they could darken.

Slow internet made some uploads take 60 to 90 seconds, and some nurses discouraged patients from joining because of the extra burden. This was an early field study, published by Google itself. The lesson is the gap between test and clinic: test it where it will be used.

title.text:
A good system says “not sure”
and passes the case to a person

objects.alt: A good system says “not sure” and passes the case to a person

objects.text: Ask every vendor what the tool does with a photo it cannot read.

runs.text: Makerere rebuilt its app to answer “undetermined”.
Session 0: Nuru was far better on six leaves than on one.

slides.notes:
What should a good system do with a photo it cannot read?

Admit it. Makerere’s team found that an early version of the cassava app gave answers even when pointed at things that were not plants at all. A model trained only on cassava photos will force every image into one of the labels it knows. So the team rebuilt it to answer undetermined and hand the case to a person.

You met the other half of this in Session 0: PlantVillage Nuru was right 74 to 88 times in 100 when it looked at six leaves of a plant, and 49 in 100 on a single leaf. How the tool is used changes the score.

title.text:
From maize fields in Mbale to Uganda’s courts,
AI already reads photos, forms and speech

objects.alt: From maize fields in Mbale to Uganda’s courts, AI already reads photos, forms and speech

objects.text: Banking is the gap: we found no published case of a named bank doing this.

slides.notes:
Across the six main industries, the idea is already at work. In banking, the typical use is reading ID cards and loan forms into the system; we found no published case with a named bank, so the tile says so rather than invent one. In telecom, Orange plans speech models for customers in Wolof and Pulaar, in West Africa.

In agriculture, a developer in Mbale built a free app that spots fall armyworm on maize from a photo. In FMCG, Coca-Cola HBC’s sales reps photograph shelves, and image recognition scores the display on 60 to 70 per cent of visits, by the company’s own account. In health, Makerere’s AI Health Lab points out malaria parasites in a blood-smear photo, still in testing. And Uganda’s Judiciary bought 70 licences for court transcription.

title.text:
One Acre Fund in Burundi says form checking fell from
over 1,000 person-days to an estimated 300 to 500

objects.alt: One Acre Fund in Burundi says form checking fell from over 1,000 person-days to an estimated 300 to 500

objects.text: The software reads; people decide on what it flags.

slides.notes:
The first story reads paper. One Acre Fund supplies seed and fertiliser to smallholder farmers, and in Burundi it receives about 80,000 paper delivery forms a year, each to be checked against digital survey records. Text-reading software, the OCR from our earlier slide, now reads each scanned form and compares it with the records.

Staff look only at the entries the system flags in yellow or red. The company says the work fell from more than 1,000 person-days per cycle to an estimated 300 to 500, a cut of up to 70 per cent, and 80,000 forms went through in two to three weeks.

Two cautions: this is a vendor’s customer story, and the figure is an estimate. About 120 review staff still check what it flags.

title.text:
In Sweden’s MASAI trial, AI sorting let
radiologists read 44% less and find more cancers

objects.alt: In Sweden’s MASAI trial, AI sorting let radiologists read 44% less and find more cancers

objects.text: The AI decides who reads each scan, and a doctor still reads every one.

slides.notes:
The second story sees, and it is the strongest evidence in today’s set because it was a randomised trial. In Sweden’s breast screening programme, each mammogram is normally read by two radiologists. In the MASAI trial, AI scored each scan for cancer risk. Low-risk scans got one radiologist, high-risk scans two.

Across 80,033 women, the AI group found 41 more cancers, about 20 per cent more, with no rise in false alarms reported, and radiologists did 44 per cent less reading. The limits: these were interim results from one site, the main result needed two more years of follow-up, and the authors warn that finding more cancers can also mean treating some that would never have caused harm. Every scan still had a doctor.

title.text:
Kenya’s Chief Justice says AI now types
most court records, at about 80% accuracy

objects.alt: Kenya’s Chief Justice says AI now types most court records, at about 80% accuracy

objects.text: Speech-to-text has reached East African courtrooms.

slides.notes:
The third story hears. Every court hearing needs a written record, and in Kenya that work is moving to speech-to-text software. In August 2025 Chief Justice Martha Koome said transcription is now mainly done by AI, and put its accuracy at about 80 per cent, up from about 30 per cent when testing began.

The Judiciary’s draft policy keeps AI to support work such as transcription and research, and away from writing judgments. Those figures come from a speech and were not measured independently, and at 80 per cent a person must still check every record. Closer to home, Uganda’s Judiciary has bought 70 licences for AI transcription, so this is arriving here too.

title.text:
Watch a small network learn to read
handwritten digits, in a recorded run

objects.text: I will show

objects.alt: Watch a small network learn to read handwritten digits, in a recorded run

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: How it improves with practice
Which digits it gets wrong
What happens when the same digits move one dot

slides.notes:
Time to see the idea at work, on a task anyone can judge: reading handwritten digits. The images are 1,797 small scans of handwritten digits, each labelled with the right answer, from a public research collection. A small neural network learns from 1,347 of them and is tested on 450 it never saw.

I recorded the run on 5 November 2026 with a free tool called scikit-learn; it gives the same result every time, and I ran it twice to check. Watch how it improves with practice, which digits it gets wrong, and what happens when I move the same digits one dot to the right. That last part answers our question about trust.

title.text:
It learned from 1,347 labelled digits and
read 436 of 450 new ones correctly

objects.alt: It learned from 1,347 labelled digits and read 436 of 450 new ones correctly

objects.text: Real images and answers from the recorded run; its mistakes are untidy digits.

slides.notes:
On the 450 digits it never saw, it read 436 correctly, about 97 in 100, and got 14 wrong. The top row shows the first eight unseen digits with what the network said and what each was; all eight are right. The bottom row ends with four of its fourteen mistakes, in red: an 8 read as a 1, a 4 read as an 8, a 5 read as a 3, a 4 read as a 1.

These are untidy digits a tired clerk might misread too. Nobody told the network what a 4 looks like. It learned that from the labelled examples alone, through practice, and it needed a good deal of practice.

title.text:
With practice it improved from
17 in 100 right to 97 in 100

objects.alt: With practice it improved from 17 in 100 right to 97 in 100

objects.text: Each pass, it adjusts itself a little to match the labels. That adjusting is called training.

runs.text: Recorded run, 5 November 2026.

slides.notes:
Each bar shows how many of 100 unseen digits it read correctly after a given number of passes through its 1,347 practice digits. After one pass it got 17 in 100 right, not much better than guessing among ten digits. After ten passes, 37. After fifty, 92. After two hundred, 97.

Each pass, the network adjusts itself a little so its answers match the labels better; that adjusting is what the industry calls training. The quality comes from the examples and the practice. A vendor who cannot tell you what their system learned from cannot tell you what it will do. The next test shows why.

title.text:
Move the same digits one dot to the right,
and it reads fewer than half correctly

objects.alt: Move the same digits one dot to the right, and it reads fewer than half correctly

objects.text: A person would not notice. The network falls from 97 in 100 to 46.

runs.text: It learned digits in one position.
Test with your own photos, as they come.

slides.notes:
I took the same 450 unseen digits and moved each one dot to the right. You can barely see the difference, and a person would read every one as before. The network fell from 97 in 100 right to 46. Moved two dots, it got 14 in 100.

Every digit it learned from sat in roughly the same place, so a shift it never saw makes a new kind of image. It is the lesson of the Thai clinics and Nuru’s single leaf again: a model struggles when the new image differs from its examples. Larger systems are trained on more varied photos and cope better, but the question stays: were they trained on photos like yours?

title.text:
Live and unrecorded, an approved
assistant reads a receipt photo into a table

objects.text: I will show

objects.alt: Live and unrecorded, an approved assistant reads a receipt photo into a table

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: Which fields come out right
What it does with a smudge or a crease
Whether it says when it is unsure

slides.notes:
Now a live try, and I say live because I have not recorded it, so neither of us knows the result. I photograph a printed receipt, one with no personal details, and ask an AI assistant your organisation has approved to put the date, the items and the total into a table.

Watch which fields come out right, what it does with a smudge or a crease, and whether it says when it is unsure. Then we check every field against the paper. If the connection or the tool fails, or it refuses, the fallback is on the slide: we read the receipt into the table by hand together, and compare the steps with One Acre Fund’s software.

There is no recording, so I never describe a result we did not see.

title.text:
Radiologists, inspectors and clerks
read less routine work and check more

objects.alt: Radiologists, inspectors and clerks read less routine work and check more

objects.text: One Acre Fund’s 120 reviewers and Sweden’s radiologists still check what the tool flags.

slides.notes:
These tools change jobs before they change results, and three roles feel it first. A radiologist reads fewer routine scans and spends more time on the doubtful ones and on the patient; the skill to grow is knowing when the tool is out of its depth. An inspector or field officer walks fewer fields and shelves and follows up what the photos flag; the skill is taking photos the tool can read.

A data-entry clerk types fewer forms and checks the fields marked unsure. The fears are real: being replaced, being watched, the job going. The gains are time for hard cases and less typing. What do your clerks or inspectors fear about this today?

title.text:
When a face check says no to a person, someone
must review it and the person must be able to appeal

objects.alt: When a face check says no to a person, someone must review it and the person must be able to appeal

objects.text: A face check is an image model with a person’s livelihood behind it.

runs.text: Name who reviews each “no”.
Give an appeal route.
Check it works for every group of staff.

slides.notes:
The hardest case is when the photo is of a person. Uber Eats in the United Kingdom asks couriers for a selfie, which software compares with their account photo. After repeated mismatches, one Black courier was removed through an automated process. With support from the Equality and Human Rights Commission and a union, the courier brought a discrimination claim, which was settled in March 2024, and the courier was reinstated.

Uber says its checks have human review and that the automated check did not cause the removal, and the bias question was never tested in court. Your rule follows from it: name the person who reviews every no, and give people a way to appeal.

title.text:
Six questions to put to a vendor before
AI reads your photos, pages or recordings

rows.text: Ask
Why it matters
What photos, pages or recordings did it learn from?
It only knows the kind it was shown
Were they like ours: our cameras, forms, languages, light?
A new kind of image breaks it
How often is it right on our own samples?
The vendor’s score was on their images
What does it do with a photo it cannot read?
A good tool says “not sure”
Who checks what it flags, and who reviews a “no” about a person?
People answer for the decision
Where do our images and recordings go?
Photos and voices can be personal data

slides.notes:
Everything so far comes down to six questions, one per row, for your team as much as for a vendor. Ask what photos, pages or recordings it learned from, because it only knows the kind it was shown. Ask whether they were like yours: your cameras, your forms, your languages, your light.

Ask how often it is right on a sample of your own, since the vendor’s score was measured on their images; Session 3 shows how to read that score. Ask what it does with a photo it cannot read. Ask who checks what it flags, and who reviews a no about a person.

And ask where your images and recordings go, because faces and voices can be personal data; check that point with your lawyer.

title.text:
Add one place where AI could see or read
for you to your AI Opportunity Portfolio

objects.text: 25 minutes
Hands-on: your portfolio
Find a pile of photos, paper or recordings that people in your organisation look at by hand.

runs.text: Name the pile and who handles it today.
Fill the five columns, as in the example.
Add today’s column: what it sees or reads, and what happens to poor images.
Write one question for the vendor.

objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: One or two portfolio entries, each with its poor-image rule.

slides.notes:
For twenty-five minutes you work on your own organisation, and I walk round. Open the AI Opportunity Portfolio in your workbook. Look for a pile that people handle by eye or by hand today: delivery notes, invoices, ID copies, meter photos, shelf photos, X-rays, call recordings or meeting minutes.

Name the pile and who handles it. Fill the five columns: the use, what goes in, what comes out, who uses it, and how you would know it works. Then today’s column: what it sees or reads, and what happens to a poor image. The example on the right is for Nile Valley Foods, our fictional distributor. Finish with one question you would put to a vendor.

title.text:
Which pile of photos, paper or speech in
your organisation would you start with?

objects.text: Of the uses you just wrote, which would you start with, and why?

objects.alt: doc

objects.text: Paper to data
Forms, invoices or delivery notes typed in by hand today

objects.alt: magnifier

objects.text: Photos to check
Shelves, crops, meters or damage that inspectors look at

objects.alt: speech

objects.text: Speech to text
Meetings, hearings or calls that someone writes up

objects.alt: clock

objects.text: Not yet
Our images vary too much, or no one could check the results
Write your decision and the reason in your workbook.

slides.notes:
With your entries written, one decision. Paper to data, if forms, invoices or delivery notes are typed in by hand today. Photos to check, if inspectors or reps spend their days looking at shelves, crops, meters or damage. Speech to text, if meetings, hearings or calls are written up by someone.

Or not yet, if your images vary too much or no one could check the results; that is an honest answer, and your first step becomes collecting good examples. One Acre Fund chose a pile with high volume where a person could check what was flagged. I will ask three of you for your choice and the pile it works on.

title.text:
A model that sees or reads is only as
good as the examples it learned from

objects.alt: A model that sees or reads is only as good as the examples it learned from

objects.text: Our network read 97 in 100 new digits, and 46 in 100 once they moved one dot.

runs.text: Photos, pages and speech share one idea.
Test any tool on your own samples.
A person checks what it flags.

slides.notes:
If you remember one image from today, make it this one. The network learned from labelled examples and read 97 in 100 new digits; moved one dot, the same digits fell to 46. Everything else follows from it. Photos, pages and speech are one idea, learning from examples experts have labelled, so all three are strong on volume and weak when the new image differs from what they learned.

That is why you test any tool on your own samples, messy ones included, and why a person checks what it flags and reviews every no about a person.

title.text:
Keep the sheet, and the seeing or
reading use you added to your portfolio

objects.text: What you keep from today

runs.text: A one-page sheet: one idea behind seeing, reading and hearing, when it struggles, the questions to ask, today’s recorded results, and your new portfolio entry.

objects.text: Our question today
What can AI see or read for us, and when should we not trust what it sees?
Next session
Session 2: AI that predicts from your data.

objects.alt: What you keep from today

slides.notes:
Keep the take-away sheet. It holds the one idea behind seeing, reading and hearing, the ways it struggles, the questions for your team and your vendor, and today’s recorded numbers: 436 of 450 new digits read correctly, and only 46 in 100 once the same digits moved one dot.

Your portfolio now holds a place where AI could see or read for you. In Session 2 the same learning from labelled examples turns to the records you already keep: who will repay, order, leave or break down next.

We began with this question: What can AI see or read for us, and when should we not trust what it sees? Before you go, say in one sentence what you can now say about it.
